source.title: Relationship between food waste, diet quality, and environmental sustainability

analysis.summary: This 2018 research article combines US dietary survey data, national food-loss estimates, and biophysical modeling to examine consumer-level food waste and its relationship with diet quality and agricultural resource use. Estimated daily waste was 422 g per person, with approximately 30 million acres of cropland used annually to produce uneaten food. Higher Healthy Eating Index-2015 scores were associated with more estimated food waste and greater embodied irrigation-water and pesticide use, but less embodied cropland use. These are observational, model-dependent associations rather than direct measurements of individual waste or evidence that improving diet quality causes increased waste.
analysis.studyType: Cross-sectional observational secondary-data analysis with biophysical simulation modeling
keyFindings: Estimated daily consumer food waste was 421.5 g per person (95% CI: 409.1–433.9), approximately 26% of food available by weight.
Fruits, vegetables, and their mixed dishes accounted for 38.9% of estimated waste by weight, followed by dairy (17.1%), meat and mixed meat dishes (13.5%), and grains and mixed grain dishes (12.1%).
Estimated wasted energy was approximately 817 kcal per person daily, with a reported interval of 795–840 kcal, or about 29% of available daily energy.
Producing wasted food required an estimated 30.02 million acres of cropland annually (95% CI: 29.29–30.76 million), equivalent to 7.7% of US harvested cropland.
Estimated food waste increased from 295 g/day in the lowest diet-quality quintile to 535 g/day in the highest quintile; the trend was statistically significant (P < 0.001).

Higher diet quality was associated with less embodied cropland use (P = 0.029), but greater embodied irrigation-water and pesticide use (both P < 0.001). The authors reported no corresponding association with fertilizer waste.

Annual resources embodied in wasted food included approximately 4.2 trillion gallons of irrigation water, 780 million pounds of pesticides, and 5.6 billion pounds of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potash fertilizers combined.
limitations: Food waste was inferred from reported consumption and national food-specific loss proportions, not directly measured for participants. Actual waste rates may vary across individuals and diet-quality groups in ways the analysis cannot capture.

The cross-sectional design and modeled associations do not establish causality. Applying food-specific waste proportions to dietary composition also makes estimated waste partly dependent on the foods used to characterize diet quality.
Waste estimates included cooking losses, such as fats and oils remaining in a pan; these may not fit all definitions of avoidable food waste.

Dietary intake relied on one self-reported 24-hour recall per participant. Recall and social-desirability errors could affect both diet-quality scores and waste estimates; the authors note possible overestimation from over-reporting fruits and vegetables.

The model assumed a closed US food system with all food domestically produced, excluding the actual geography and production conditions of imported foods. The authors suggest this could underestimate cropland requirements.
Only 92% of Food Commodity Intake Database foods were matched to food-loss data; unmatched foods were excluded.
Datasets covered different years, and chemical-use estimates for hay and pasture relied on communications with agricultural extension agents because survey data were unavailable.
Reported uncertainty reflects variation in dietary intake through modeling and does not necessarily encompass all uncertainty in loss rates, recipe matching, or agricultural assumptions.

Resource-use estimates are not direct measurements of environmental damage. The analysis did not comprehensively assess greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity, soil erosion, or regional differences in environmental impact.
Proposed consumer education and waste-reduction approaches were not tested for effectiveness in this study.

claims.text: US consumers wasted nearly one pound of food per person daily during 2007–2014.
claims.evidence: Linked dietary and food-loss datasets yielded 421.5 g/day (95% CI: 409.1–433.9; n = 35,507). This is an estimated population average, not directly observed household waste.

claims.text: Higher-quality diets were associated with greater food waste.
claims.evidence: Estimated waste was 295 g/day (95% CI: 282–308) in HEI-2015 quintile 1 and 535 g/day (501–568) in quintile 5, with P < 0.001 for trend. Individual waste behavior and causal effects were not measured.

claims.text: Higher diet quality had different relationships with different sustainability indicators.
claims.evidence: Regression trends indicated lower embodied cropland use (P = 0.029), higher irrigation-water and pesticide use (both P < 0.001), and no reported fertilizer association. These outcomes were derived from modeled cropland and agricultural application rates.

claims.text: Fruits and vegetables largely explain the tradeoff between lower cropland requirements and higher waste-associated water and pesticide use.
claims.evidence: Fruits, vegetables, and mixed dishes contributed 38.9% of estimated waste by weight. The authors attribute the pattern to greater inclusion in higher-quality diets, relatively high assigned waste rates, lower land requirements, and higher agricultural inputs per unit area.

claims.text: Food waste embodies substantial agricultural resource use.
claims.evidence: The modified US Foodprint Model estimated approximately 30 million acres of annual cropland use; combining modeled land areas with agricultural application rates yielded approximately 4.2 trillion gallons of irrigation water and 780 million pounds of pesticides.

claims.text: Diet-quality improvement and food-waste reduction should be considered together.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the modeled resource tradeoffs. Their proposed education, storage, labeling, and institutional approaches were not evaluated experimentally.

relevance: Useful for research on tradeoffs between nutritional quality and environmental sustainability rather than treating sustainability as a single outcome.
Provides a method for integrating dietary recalls, ingredient-level recipes, food-loss proportions, and agricultural resource modeling.
Highlights the importance of distinguishing waste by weight, calories, nutrients, land use, and agricultural inputs.
Offers historical US baseline estimates, but does not establish current waste levels or the effectiveness of particular waste-reduction interventions.
analysis.population: US individuals aged 2 years and older participating in the dietary component of NHANES, What We Eat In America, across the 2007–2008, 2009–2010, 2011–2012, and 2013–2014 survey waves.
analysis.comparator: Observational comparisons across HEI-2015 diet-quality quintiles, from lowest to highest quality; no assigned control group.
